questions.prompt: The slope-field graph below represents y′=y. Which function follows its directions throughout the real line and passes through (0,1)?
options: y=eˣ
y=1+x
questions.explanation: A solution curve must be tangent to the field at every point on the curve, not just at the initial point. For y=eˣ, y′=eˣ=y and y(0)=1. The line 1+x initially shares the same tangent but soon disagrees with the changing field directions. A: Its derivative equals its height everywhere and its initial value is 1. B: Its derivative is 1, not its changing height except at x=0. C: Its slope is negative above the axis, opposing the field. D: Its horizontal tangent disagrees with the field’s slope 1 at height 1.

questions.prompt: A solution to the equation represented by the slope-field graph below passes through (0,1). What must occur at x=0?
options: The solution has a strict local maximum.
The solution has a strict local minimum.
The solution crosses the x-axis.
No extremum occurs because all horizontal segments are in one column.
questions.explanation: The field supplies y′=2x along every solution. For x<0 the solution decreases, and for x>0 it increases. Therefore the solution has a strict local minimum at its specified point (0,1). The conclusion follows from field signs without calculating its full formula. A: That requires a positive-to-negative slope change, opposite to the field. B: Its derivative changes from negative on the left to positive on the right. C: The initial point has height 1, so it does not lie on that axis. D: The slope sign change along the solution establishes a minimum.

questions.prompt: For the solution through (1,1) in the slope-field graph below, y′=x−y. Which conclusion at x=1 is justified by differentiating the equation?
options: It has a local maximum because the field is horizontal there.
It follows y=x on an interval because that is the zero-slope line.
The solution has a strict local minimum because y′(1)=0 and y″(1)=1.
Its concavity cannot be determined even from the stated equation.
questions.explanation: At (1,1), y′=1−1=0. Differentiating y′=x−y along the solution gives y″=1−y′, hence y″(1)=1>0. The second-derivative test establishes a strict local minimum. The zero-slope locus is not itself a solution curve. A: A horizontal tangent alone does not establish a maximum. B: The line y=x has derivative 1, not the required zero along that line. C: The second-derivative test applies at this stationary point. D: Differentiating gives y″=1−y′, which is determined at the initial point.

questions.prompt: A solution of y′=−y starts at y(0)=3. Which description is consistent with this smooth field for all x≥0?
options: It crosses y=0 and then continues decreasing into negative values.
It increases without bound because its initial value is positive.
It stays at height 3 because each horizontal row has a repeated slope.
It remains positive and decreases toward 0.
questions.explanation: The horizontal field at y=0 is an equilibrium solution. For this particular smooth equation, the initial-value solution is 3e^(−x), which is positive, decreasing and tends to zero. Repeated row slopes do not make nonzero constant functions into solutions. A: The unique solution never reaches zero at a finite x; below zero the field would point upward. B: Positive height gives negative derivative in this equation. C: The repeated slope at height 3 is −3, not zero. D: The solution 3e^(−x) has negative slope and approaches zero from above.

questions.prompt: For y′=1+y², what can be concluded about any real solution on its interval of existence?
options: It is strictly increasing throughout that interval.
It is concave up throughout every interval.
It has a horizontal tangent whenever y=0.
It must exist for every real x because every field slope is finite.
questions.explanation: Because 1+y²≥1>0, every solution has positive derivative wherever it exists and is therefore strictly increasing. This conclusion concerns its interval of existence. Positive first derivative alone gives no universal concavity or global-domain conclusion. A: The derivative is at least 1 for every real y. B: Since y″=2y(1+y²), concavity depends on the sign of y. C: At height zero the derivative is 1, not zero. D: Finite slopes at individual points do not guarantee global existence; solutions can become unbounded.

questions.prompt: In the field for y′=y−2, consider a solution with y(0)=5. How does it behave as x increases?
options: It decreases toward y=2 from above.
It stays above y=2 and moves upward away from that equilibrium.
It crosses y=2 and continues below it.
It remains at y=5.
questions.explanation: The row y=2 is horizontal, but above it y′ is positive. The solution through height 5 is y=2+3eˣ: its difference from 2 stays positive and increases. Thus it moves away from the equilibrium as x grows; the repeated row structure does not imply a constant solution at height 5. A: Above 2 the derivative is positive, so downward motion contradicts the field. B: The solution is 2+3eˣ, so its excess above 2 grows. C: Its explicit excess above 2 is always positive. D: At height 5 the field slope is 3, not zero.

questions.prompt: A solution of y′=2xy passes through (0,−1). What type of stationary point does it have there?
options: A strict local minimum
No stationary point because the height is negative
A strict local maximum
A point on the constant solution y=0
questions.explanation: At the initial point, y′=2·0·(−1)=0. Differentiate the equation by the product rule: y″=2y+2xy′. At x=0 this equals −2, so the second-derivative test gives a strict local maximum even though its height is negative. A: The second derivative is negative, not positive. B: Stationarity is determined by the derivative, not the height. C: At x=0 the slope is zero and y″=2y+2xy′ equals −2. D: The initial value −1 is incompatible with that constant solution.

questions.prompt: The slope-field graph below represents y′=−x/y. A solution passes through (0,2). Which description is correct near that point?
options: It has a vertical tangent because x=0.
It is concave up because y is positive.
It follows the constant line y=2.
It has a horizontal tangent and is concave down.
questions.explanation: At (0,2), y′=−0/2=0. Differentiate y y′=−x to obtain (y′)²+y y″=−1. Substituting y=2 and y′=0 yields y″=−1/2. Therefore a local solution has a horizontal tangent and is concave down. A: The denominator is y=2, so the slope is the finite value zero. B: Concavity depends on the derivative relation, which gives a negative value here. C: That line would have zero derivative everywhere, but −x/2 is not identically zero. D: The derivative is zero there, and differentiating the equation gives y″(0)=−1/2.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows slope segments only at integer grid points in a square. No formula for the differential equation is provided. Which claim can be made from that finite diagram alone?
options: It records local tangent directions at the displayed points.
It determines the equation uniquely among all possible smooth formulas.
It proves every solution stays bounded for all real x.
It determines one solution without an initial point.
questions.explanation: A finite field displays selected values of a differential right side. It helps visualize solution behavior, but without additional information it does not uniquely determine an arbitrary formula, prove global bounds or select one initial-value solution. Interpret the diagram at its actual level of evidence. A: That is the defined information encoded by a finite slope field. B: Different formulas can agree on every finite grid point and differ between them. C: The diagram gives neither global-domain information nor all intermediate slopes. D: A field usually represents directions for many curves; an initial condition selects a particular one when uniqueness holds.

questions.prompt: Two proposed differentiable solution curves of y′=x+y meet at (1,2). What must be true about their tangent lines at that point?
options: One must have slope 1 and the other slope 2.
Both tangent lines have slope 3.
They must cross at right angles.
Their tangent slopes depend on their earlier heights.
questions.explanation: Every solution through (1,2) must satisfy y′=1+2=3 at that point. Thus both proposed tangents coincide in direction. The statement follows immediately from the field’s single slope at that point; it does not require assuming a general uniqueness theorem for arbitrary equations. A: The separate coordinates are not separate derivative choices. B: The right side assigns the same slope 1+2 to any solution passing through that point. C: The field assigns one slope there, so perpendicular tangents are impossible. D: The right side here depends only on the current coordinates.

questions.prompt: For the solution of y′=x²+y with y(1)=2, which line is tangent at the initial point?
questions.explanation: The field gives the instantaneous slope at the initial point: 1²+2=3. Point-slope form then gives y−2=3(x−1). This tangent line describes local direction; it is not claimed to be the exact solution away from the initial point. A: This uses the height as slope and omits x². B: This has the wrong height at x=1 and the wrong slope. C: The slope is 1²+2=3 and the line passes through (1,2). D: This reverses the field direction at the initial point.
